speaker: donanderson
text: Thank you. Well, the first item on the agenda is proclamations and presentations. And the first item of business there isn't always joyous because we're losing a great party partner of the city of Lakewood. And we'd like that this time to recognize Colonel retired Thomas G Knight, the chief staff retiring at JBLM. Greetings, Tom. Thanks for joining us. So as I indicated, just as a background over the last 14 years, the city of Lakewood has had the opportunity to work with Tom Knight, kind of the glue that was holding things together of continuity, at least at JBLM as a senior civilian employee at JBLM working in the Harrison command office. And Tom has retired once as a Colonel from the United States Army. And he's retiring again from a civil service position. Worst thing I can say about him is he lives in Lacey. But I'd like to read this proclamation on behalf of the city council. Whereas Thomas G Knight, Colonel retired United States Army achieved extraordinary accomplishments encompassing more than 44 years in federal service culminating as the Joint Base Chief of Staff for Joint Base Lewis-McChord. And whereas his services as a highly decorated officer in the United States Army spanned 30 years and included assignments with infantry, special forces and civil military operations units. Whereas during his 30 years of service he received many decorations and badges to include the Legion of Merit, Bronze Star Medal, the Defense Meritorious Service Medal, Meritorious Service Medal, Joint Service Commendation Medal, Joint Service Achievement Medal, Army Commendation Medal, Army Achievement Medal, CIB, which is Combat Infantry Badge, CAB, EIB, Master Parachute Badge, Special Forces Tab, SCUBA Badge and the Pathfinder Badge. And whereas Colonel retired Knight is a graduate of the National Defense University's National War College and the US Air Force Air Command and Staff College holding a doctorate in public administration and advanced degrees in political science, international relations and national security strategy. And whereas the Joint Base Chief of Staff as the Joint Base Chief of Staff uses many talents to provide superb leadership advice and continuity to six garrison commanders, eight army and air force senior service component commanders and to a civilian workforce of over 2,483 employees. And whereas Colonel Knight's outstanding federal civilian service spans from 2007 through 2021 totaling over 14 years. And whereas Colonel Knight is universally recognized for his uncompromising values and ethical foundation for leading by example, sound reasoning and creative skills for solving complex challenges and problems associated with providing mission essential services. Whereas Colonel Knight worked tirelessly with the city of Lakewood and surrounding leaders to promote community relations and negotiated hundreds of solutions to share challenges with mutually beneficial outcomes for the entire region. And whereas he was instrumental in the formulation and establishment of the South Sound Military and Community Partnerships supporting, establishing and leading many initiatives to benefit our service members and their families. And whereas through his SSMCP leadership role, he enabled the partnership to establish and pursue legislative priorities for the state of Washington that resulted in a $500 million I-5 corridor improvement project that will alleviate traffic congestion near JBLM by increasing the roadway capacity in each direction through the six mile JBLM corridor. Whereas Colonel Knight provided the leadership to develop a memorandum of agreement that outlines the action plan to resolve encroachment in the McCord North Clear Zone. And whereas Colonel Knight was instrumental in partnering with the city of Lakewood and SSMCP that resulted in the creation and funding of a new federal law, the Defense Community Infrastructure Program, DSIP. And whereas Colonel Knight also guided SSMCP to secure Office of Economic Adjustment funding to address traffic, housing affordability and availability for military services in their family, impact of light pollution on flight and many other military training operations. And whereas during his tenure as Joint Base Chief of Staff, Colonel Knight administered the investment of over $2 billion in federal funds, MilCon money in a wide range of significant military construction projects on JBLM, ranging from transportation, housing, barracks, six elementary schools, training facilities and recreation amenities that address and ensure our service members and their families are properly taken care of. And whereas Colonel Knight's exceptional career helped make JBLM the premier and most diverse installation within the Department of Defense, the station of choice for both Army and Air Force service members and a committed partner to the city of Lakewood and the surrounding communities. Now, therefore the city of Lakewood Council and the citizens of the city of Lakewood hereby express their deepest appreciation for Thomas G. Knight, Colonel retired U.S. Army for his exemplary accomplishments and for setting the standards for which quality leadership of civilian and military should aspire to emulate proclaimed the 17th of May, 2021, Don Anderson Mayor. Tom, we'll give you a virtual round of applause and you can unmute your mic and floor is yours.

speaker: tedhill
text: Great. Welcome. Thank you. Again, Ted Hill, Capital Projects Division Manager. So tonight, the six year tip, which you all saw last week. So the city is updating the six year Comprehensive Transportation Improvement Program or the six year tip. Updating the program is an annual process required by state statute, meant to assure continued consistency with comprehensive planning goals and to evaluate current transportation needs. The public hearing tonight is an important part of the process, affording the public an opportunity to comment on the program prior to its adoption. The final draft of the tip was developed over the past few months. It outlines over $176 million in transportation related capital improvement projects the city intends to pursue over the next six years and beyond. The program does not include routine operation and maintenance activities or WSDOT led projects. Those functions are taken care of outside of this program or funded by others. The six year tip is a planning level document. And as such, the program is not fiscally balanced with respect to the current anticipated city revenues. Implementation of the tip occurs through the city's biannual budget and the capital improvement program process. Recent grants have helped to maintain a healthy capital improvement program. Projects must be included in the city's current tip in order to be eligible to receive most transportation related project funding grants. This draft tip was presented to the council last Monday, May 10th, during the state session. In addition, the document is on the city's website and a request for comment will be made through social media. Any comments received tonight through public hearing or via social media will be reviewed and evaluated by staff. Any required modifications can be incorporated into the final six year tip, which is currently scheduled for adoption at the June 7th council meeting. In December, the City Council gave direction to select a new artist and a new process was recommended to use public art rosters to create a shortlist rather than sending out an RFP. Also, a new selection panel was created, and it's a public art subcommittee, and it has two City Council reps on it and a Youth Council representative, as well as business owners and members of the Lakewood community. So it's very well organized. In May, City Council gave direction to increase the budget up to 150,000, and that was to allow for the expense of installation, engineering, and restoration. In March, 20 artists were selected, and of those, 12 opted in. Their portfolios were requested, 10 slides each, resumes, et cetera, and those were reviewed by the selection panel. And from there, they were selected by the selection panel, and from there, six finalists were selected. In April, those six artists were invited to an onsite orientation at Colonial Plaza, where they learned firsthand from staff about the history and especially about the future plans at Colonial Plaza. The artists then were invited to give a presentation to the public art subcommittee on what ideas they generated from that onsite visit and what they might do at that space. From there, in May, three finalists were selected, and they are John Fleming, Laura Haddad, and Thomas Drogan, their husband-wife team, and Peter Requim. They're currently preparing two design concepts each and being paid a stipend of $1,500. In June, they'll be presenting their work to the public art subcommittee in the last week of June. And in July, the public art subcommittee will make a recommendation to the arts commission at the July meeting. Following consensus, the arts commission will forward a recommendation to city council. It will include the selected artists, design, the project budget, and timeline. In July, August, and early September, the artists will be given feedback to hone that final design. And in September, a contract for public art will be created and the artwork produced. We're thrilled to be on target for the timeline. And I'm gonna talk a little bit about why we chose each artist. So John Fleming has a wonderful use of lighting, and he was the only artist that spoke about the 25th anniversary art contest. So he'd really done his homework. He went to the website. He looked at it. He was really intrigued by that and how it spoke to the diversity in the community and the theme of unity. He was eager to talk to our sister cities and do more research about this if he was selected. He suggested the use of bronze to warm up the space. He also suggested the idea of having something movable so that you didn't have to have the expense of securing it. He showed clever uses of saving money and letting the budget go farther, for example, using recycled materials. And his pieces are both interactive and can be seen from a distance, which is something that we're looking for in this piece at the Colonial Plaza. He shows the ability to bring the history of an area into his artwork. And this is an example. This is called Redmond's Erratic. And he looked way back into the history where they had these glacial formations and he incorporated those into his art. So we were excited about his ability to really look into the history and create artwork that is interactive and engaging with the community. His past pieces are statement pieces as well and include great use of lighting. The Hada Jurgen team are amazing. They're known for their very large, elegant and grandly lit pieces. The committee was very impressed that they did their homework and their research. And they spoke a lot about the art being a precursor of what is to come at Colonial Plaza. So in a way, the artwork is really setting the stage for what's to come next. They are the ones that suggested the very clever use of the Gary Oaks as you come in on the right-hand side on the lawn and uplighting them and using them as a natural gateway as an inexpensive and effective way to call attention to the area. They do draw inspiration from the area. So their artwork is very site-specific and they showed an ability to do a really wide array of shapes and sizes. They're really known for using natural elements like the sun and wind to change and make their work really dynamic as the day moves on. And their artwork's very responsive to the environment. It's iconic at a distance and eye-catching, but up close it has texture and is engaging. Peter Requim, and don't be scared by this, he has a very definitive style and he uses humor and whimsy. And this particular piece was for a fast food restaurant. It wasn't for a municipality, but he does his homework. He had driven out to go to the Historical Society and really dig down deep. It had been closed, but that's the type of person he is. And all the artists will be going to the Historical Society shortly to do more homework and learn more about Lakewood. But what he has is the unique ability to really distill the essence of a place into a piece of artwork. It's really rather amazing. And he has a very strong sense of community engagement. So while his pieces would have a very unique flavor to the city of Lakewood, and the committee did appreciate that he could tell us what was unique about Lakewood. So what did we learn from the artist interviews? It was a very insightful process. One thing that we learned from them is they really felt that the pavers were artwork themselves and it is true. We did find out that to build on the cement, so if you are looking at the theater and the pavers are in front of it, if you follow it to the right, then there's a point at which it becomes the cement slabs and that is the point at which some of the artists envisioned art and we would need an adjustment to the easement for that. text: Council member Farber, long story short, the answer is yes. We actually expect to continue to allow, for example, public comment and public testimony, for example, through public hearings to include, to occur via Zoom or the telephone as well.

speaker: lindafarmer
text: Fantastic.

speaker: johncaulfield
text: Thank you. Actually, unless the council has any objection to that.

speaker: mikikebrandstetter
text: Mr. Bransfetter. Yes, Mr. Mayor, Mr. Caulfield, you mentioned we would be moving to a situation of where we would continue to be allowing employees who wanted to work remotely. And I was a little bit unsure, where are we placing the decision as to whether an employee can work remotely? Are we placing it with the employee or with the department head or with you? You know, how is that being managed?

speaker: johncaulfield
text: Council member Bransfetter, the way our current policy works, actually we were making some minor refinements to it right now, but generally speaking, the way it works, if the employee is interested in working remotely, she or he will make that request through their chain of command. The department director will then review and make a recommendation to the HR director who in turn will make a recommendation to myself. It's not something that the employee says, I wanna do this and I get to do it. It's based on the employee gets to request it. And if it serves in the best interest of the city as an organization and how we deliver services, then we will allow it. If it does not, we will not allow it. One of the caveats, for example, is a couple of examples here. For example, you have some internet activity problems or connectivity issues, maybe in your area, your wifi has gone down. Okay, pack it up and come into the office. You have some computer problems, there's some computer issues and it might take a little bit for those to be resolved. Okay, that's fine, pack it up and come into the office. So that's how we plan on addressing it. So it'll be at the request of the employee, but upon the approval of the employer.

speaker: mikikebrandstetter
text: So is there going to be a, when we have employees working remotely now, but is there gonna be some announced date that says if you want to continue working remotely after July 1st, that you have to submit a request in accordance with the existing policy that always existed for remote work.

speaker: johncaulfield
text: At Council Member Branstadter, we're working on that right now. I've already communicated to all of our employees that we plan on reopening on July 1. And right now we're reviewing and finalizing our policy, revising it, making some updates based on where the world is today. And then we expect to have that completed in the next week or so. And then that will then be made available to all employees the beginning part of June. And then our goal is to try and have that all ironed out by the middle to latter part of June. Though that doesn't mean that an employee can't come back at a later date and request it.

speaker: mikikebrandstetter
text: And are you considering that this may require an MOU

speaker: johncaulfield
text: with one or more bargaining units? Council Member Branstadter, at this point in time, no, we do not. Okay, thank you.
